name: Brittany Pettersen

summary.text: Brittany Pettersen is the incumbent U.S. Representative for Colorado's 7th Congressional District, first elected in 2022.

She previously served in the Colorado House of Representatives (28th district) and the Colorado Senate (22nd district), and earned a B.A. in political science from Metropolitan State University of Denver.
In the 119th Congress she sits on the House Financial Services Committee, including its Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance.

experience.text: Colorado State Senate, District 22, prior to election to Congress.
Worked for New Era Colorado, a nonprofit focused on youth civic participation, before running for state representative.
B.A. in political science, Metropolitan State University of Denver.

record.title: H.R. 1, One Big Beautiful Bill Act, motion to concur in Senate amendment (final passage)
record.detail: Voted No. The bill passed 218-214 and was signed into law.

record.title: S. 5, Laken Riley Act, passage
record.detail: Marked Not Voting. The bill passed 263-156.

record.title: H.R. 28, Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025, passage
record.detail: Marked Not Voting. The bill passed 218-206.

record.title: H.J. Res. 72, terminating the national emergency underlying tariffs on Canada
record.detail: Voted Yea. The resolution passed 219-211 with six Republicans joining nearly all Democrats.

record.title: Stop the Import of Fentanyl Act
record.detail: Introduced as her first bill; would create a DEA-housed national center to track and stop the import of fentanyl and other synthetic drugs.

record.title: Letter to Interior Secretary and BLM opposing rescission of the 2024 Public Lands Rule
record.detail: Joined Sen. Hickenlooper, Sen. Bennet, and Reps. DeGette, Neguse and Crow in a letter urging DOI to keep the BLM conservation rule in place.

record.title: Statement after House passage of a three-year extension of enhanced ACA premium tax credits
record.detail: Released a statement after a discharge-petition-forced House vote extended the subsidies; House passed the bill 230-196.

record.title: Bipartisan resolution allowing proxy voting for new parents in Congress
record.detail: Co-sponsored after the birth of her second son; the proposal led to a high-profile dispute with Speaker Mike Johnson. Exact introduction date not given by the source (only 'last year' relative to the October 2026 article).

positions.source_title: Colorado U.S. House District 7 candidate Q&A - The Denver Post
positions.quote: We need a system that deports convicted, dangerous criminals. Instead, Americans are being shot in the streets, families torn apart by masked, unidentified agents, and deaths in ICE custody have reached their highest level in over a decade.
positions.note: Supports deporting convicted, dangerous criminals while opposing current broad enforcement; coded disagree, the same as other candidates who take this position.

positions.source_title: Colorado U.S. House District 7 candidate Q&A - The Denver Post
positions.quote: I oppose expanding oil and gas leasing on federal lands, especially when it threatens the health of our landscapes or the communities that depend on them.
positions.note: From the Denver Post's 2026 candidate questionnaire, answering a question about opening more federal land in Colorado to oil and gas extraction.

positions.quote: Brittany is pro-choice, supported by Planned Parenthood and NARAL, and has been recognized as a champion for reproductive health care nationally.
positions.note: Page is undated; same campaign issues page as the clean-energy citation, still live on her current site.

positions.source_title: HB22-1326, Fentanyl Accountability And Prevention (Colorado General Assembly)
positions.quote: changing the criminal penalties associated with synthetic opiates; using a substance abuse assessment to direct appropriate treatment at sentencing
positions.note: Pettersen was a Senate prime sponsor. The law changed fentanyl penalties (possession of more than 1 gram of a fentanyl compound became a felony) and paired them with treatment and harm-reduction funding; it kept a 1-gram threshold rather than making any amount a felony, which is what Proposition 132 would do. Coded as mixed. No statement by her on Proposition 132 was found.

research_notes: S.5 (Laken Riley Act, 1/22/2025) and H.R. 28 (Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act, 1/14/2025) both show Pettersen as Not Voting on clerk.house.gov; Wikipedia's 'proxy voting' section explains she had just given birth to her second son and the House had not given her a proxy-voting accommodation, so no position could be sourced from either vote despite both being named in the assignment. No House floor vote occurred on the 2025 BLM land-sale amendment; it was stripped by the Rules Committee before reaching the floor, so public-lands is sourced from news coverage of a joint Democratic statement rather than a vote (clean-energy-shift, a related but distinct statement about oil/gas leasing and drilling, is instead sourced from her answer in the Denver Post's 2026 candidate Q&A, which also covers deportation-priority). No sourced position found for: graduated-income-tax, income-tax-cap, keep-tabor-surplus, conservation-sales-tax, natural-gas-right, housing-state-zoning, sports-biological-sex, minor-gender-surgery-ban, immigration-notify-ice, fentanyl-penalties, child-trafficking-life, hunting-right, mail-ballot-id, plain-language-ballots, redistricting-commission, keep-mail-voting, challenge-federal-policies (reviewer should double check these, especially redistricting-commission given a 2026 Colorado Sun story on a Democratic-aligned mid-decade redistricting push affecting her own district, where no individual Pettersen quote could be found). The abortion-legal quote from brittanypettersen.com/issues comes from an undated page whose content reads as 2022-cycle; reviewer should check whether a more current statement exists. The Denver Post/Daily Camera 2026 candidate Q&A (same article, two URLs) is the single best source for this race: it directly quotes Pettersen and Sallis (the only two who returned the questionnaire) and confirms Tim Bennett, Susan Hall, Lawrence Kyle Clark, and Joe Krzeczkowski did not. The WebSearch tool hit its session budget partway through research; the coordinator's tip to use Google News RSS (news.google.com/rss/search) and outlet site-search pages (coloradosun.com/?s=, denverpost.com/?s=) recovered good sources afterward, including this Q&A. Second pass 2026-10-14: re-read the Denver Post Q&A in full and checked the Colorado Sun's election-guide hub (coloradosun.com/2026/09/29/colorado-election-guide-2026/) and its linked ballot-measure explainers for any CD-7 candidate quotes; none mention Pettersen or Sallis by name, and no Colorado Sun CD-7 candidate guide exists (confirmed via coloradosun.com/?s= site search), so no new positions were added. Gap fill 2026-10-15: Added a mixed position on fentanyl penalties from the 2022 law she sponsored in the state Senate. The Denver Post CD7 Q&A was read again; it covers tariffs, public lands and immigration, all already coded.
